about: IB Mathematics AI SL and AI HL statements. Codes are the AI guide's own numbers (1.1 to 5.18), which differ from AA's. 'shared' lists AI codes whose content matches an AA statement: those reuse the AA statement's id, title and content (an AI HL 1.11 question and an AA 1.8 question test the same thing). 'statements' holds the AI-only content. AI SL = everything listed for ai-sl; AI HL = everything listed for ai-hl. Content is summarised from the guide; ids are permanent and shared with Wasteland Academy. The tagging rules in data/syllabus.json apply.
rules: Tag each part by what earns its marks in the markscheme, not by every piece of arithmetic or GDC use along the way.
List the primary statement first. Most parts need 1-2 tags; never more than 3.
Prior learning (rearranging, simple percentages, unit conversions, Pythagoras, reading a value off a table) is never tagged on its own.

Technology is normal in AI: tag the mathematics the GDC is used for. Zeros, intersections and solving f(x) = k from a graph, including when a model in context reaches a value, are 2.4 (with the model's own statement). A maximum or minimum read off the graph of a given function is 2.4 too, but one found from f'(x) = 0 is 5.6 and an optimum in context is 5.7. Solving a stated polynomial equation or a system of linear equations is 1.8. TVM-solver finance is 1.4 or 1.7.
If a part says 'hence' and reuses an earlier result, tag only the new content.

shared.tagWhen: Arithmetic sequences and series, as in AA: u_n, S_n, d, sigma notation and arithmetic models, including simple interest (the yearly interest on the original sum is the common difference) and judging whether an arithmetic model fits imperfect data or breaks down (negative values, non-integer n). Interest compounded on a growing balance and percentage depreciation are 1.4, regular payments are 1.7, and non-money percentage growth is 1.3; comparing simple with compound interest is 1.2 with 1.4.

subtags.name: Use simple interest as the common difference of an arithmetic model

shared.tagWhen: Any finite geometric sequence or series: a term, the general term, the sum, or a quantity growing or shrinking by a constant factor over whole periods. Money contexts (compound interest, depreciation, the TVM solver) are 1.4, regular payments are 1.7, and a sum to infinity is 1.11 at HL.

A single sum under compound interest or annual depreciation, by the formula or the TVM solver with PMT = 0: future or present value, the rate, the time to reach a target (rounded up to a whole number of compounding periods), comparing options or compounding frequencies, and the real value after inflation. As soon as there are regular payments, deposits or withdrawals (PMT ≠ 0: loans, mortgages, savings plans, annuities) the part is 1.7, even when inflation is also involved (add 1.4 only if the inflation adjustment earns its own mark); geometric growth that is not money is 1.3.

Integer exponents, converting between exponential and log form, or evaluating a log (with technology). At HL, rational exponents are 1.10 and the laws of logarithms 1.9; solving an exponential equation with the GDC inside a model is 2.4 with the model's statement.

AI HL sums to infinity, as in AA 1.8: the condition |r| < 1, S∞ = u₁/(1 − r), finding u₁ or r from a given sum, deciding whether a total has a limit, and long-run totals in context (a height that never exceeds k, the total length of a fractal, a drug level as n → ∞). A finite sum is 1.3 (1.4 or 1.7 for money); when the ratio is complex, the modulus work is 1.12 or 1.13 second.

A key feature of a graph, found from a printed graph or (usually) the GDC: zeros and intercepts, a maximum or minimum, an asymptote, symmetry, or where two graphs meet. In AI this includes solving f(x) = g(x) or f(x) = k graphically for any function, for example when a model reaches a value, every solution in an interval, or how long a function stays above a level; in a model question 2.4 goes with the model statement (2.5 or 2.9) when the model's form or context also earns marks. Solving a stated polynomial equation or a linear system with the GDC's solver is 1.8, a maximum or minimum from f′(x) = 0 is 5.6 and an optimisation problem in context is 5.7 even when the GDC finds the optimum, two straight lines meeting is 2.1, a trigonometric equation outside a model is 3.8 at HL, and reading other values off a graph is 2.3.

subtags.name: Find the interval or length of time for which a function exceeds a value

shared.tagWhen: Describing or applying translations, reflections in the axes and vertical or horizontal stretches to y = f(x), alone or in sequence: writing the transformed function, finding the image of a point, sketching the new graph, or finding the transformations or translation vector that map one graph onto another. Moving points or shapes with a matrix is 3.9; finding a sinusoidal model's parameters is 2.5 or 2.9 unless the part asks for the transformation itself; when a transformed graph feeds an area or volume, tag that integral (5.5 or 5.12) and add 2.8 only for the marks the transformation earns.

Distance or midpoint in 3D, the volume or surface area of a solid (prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, spheres, hemispheres and combinations, as in tents and containers), or the angle between two lines or a line and a plane in a solid; a plane distance that is the whole point of a part also takes SL3.1.distance-3d. Setting up a volume or surface area in one variable to optimise is 5.7 (add 3.1 if the formula earns marks), volumes by integration are 5.12, a sector folded into a cone is 3.4 or 3.7, and distances or angles found with vectors are 3.10 or 3.13.

subtags.name: Find the volume or surface area of a prism or cylinder

shared.tagWhen: Angles of elevation or depression, bearings (including one worked out from coordinates or a velocity vector), or a worded navigation or surveying triangle that needs a labelled diagram; list 3.2 with it when right-angled trigonometry or the sine or cosine rule earns the marks. The angle between a line and a plane inside a solid is 3.1; with vectors add 3.10 or 3.12 for the vector work, and when an angle of elevation only sets up a related-rates or optimisation function the calculus statement comes first.

Populations and samples, discrete and continuous data, sampling techniques (simple random, convenience, systematic, quota, stratified: naming, describing, evaluating, and the numbers in a stratified sample), bias and the reliability of data sources, or deciding in context whether to keep an outlier. Testing for an outlier with 1.5 × IQR is 4.2; at HL, designing a survey, test-retest or parallel-forms reliability and content or criterion validity are 4.12, even when the answer is about the sample.

Pearson's r with technology and its description (strength, direction, linearity), scatter diagrams, a line of best fit through the mean point, the y-on-x regression line, predicting y from it and judging the prediction (interpolation or extrapolation, strength of r, and that a y-on-x line cannot predict x, as AI has no x-on-y line), and interpreting a and b in context. R² (including r² for a linear model) and non-linear regression are 4.13, Spearman's rs is 4.10, a test of ρ = 0 is 4.18, and a regression line fitted to log-transformed data is 2.10 with 4.4.

Using a Venn, tree or sample-space diagram or a table of outcomes, combined or mutually exclusive events, independence, or a conditional probability, whether read from a diagram or found with P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) (including reversed conditionals and conditions on a random variable such as P(X = 6 | X ≥ 3)). AI keeps all of this in 4.6: AI 4.11 is χ² and t-tests, never conditional probability; the distribution supplying the probabilities (4.7, 4.8, 4.9 or 4.17) is added only when finding them earns its own marks.

subtags.name: Find P(A | B) with the formula, including reversed conditionals
Find a conditional probability for a discrete, binomial or normal random variable

shared.tagWhen: Differentiating sums of axⁿ with n an integer (negative powers included, after rewriting terms such as 980/t² or 32/x as powers), and using that derivative for a gradient at a point, a point with a given gradient or unknown coefficients from gradient conditions. In AI any other function (rational powers such as √x, sin, cos, eˣ, ln, or products and quotients) is 5.9, never both for the same derivative; AA's note 'anything else is 5.6' does not apply, because AI 5.6 is stationary points. A turning point found from the derivative adds 5.6, an optimisation 5.7 and a tangent or normal 5.4.

Anti-differentiating sums of axⁿ with n an integer, n ≠ −1 (negative powers included), finding the constant from a boundary condition (such as P from dP/dx and one known profit), writing down a definite integral for an area and evaluating it with technology, the area between a curve and the x-axis where f(x) > 0 (including areas added, subtracted or between two curves on the GDC), and the definite integral of a rate read as a total change. A definite integral evaluated on the GDC is 5.5 whatever the integrand, except that at HL an area below the x-axis or against the y-axis, or a volume, is 5.12 and a distance or displacement is 5.13; integrating anything beyond integer powers by hand is 5.11, never both for the same integral, and a trapezoidal estimate is 5.8.

subtags.name: Find an area between two curves, or by subtracting areas

shared.tagWhen: Kinematics along a straight line with scalar displacement (s or x), velocity v and acceleration a (HL only): differentiating s or v (dot notation included) and integrating v or a with an initial condition, when the particle is at rest or changes direction, distance travelled as ∫|v| dt (usually on the GDC), the greatest speed or acceleration or where the acceleration is zero, and a = v dv/ds. Tag 5.13 alone for the GDC work in these parts, adding 5.9 or 5.11 only when a product, chain or quotient rule or an inspection integral earns its own marks; motion with position or velocity vectors is 3.12, a differential equation for the motion is 5.14 to 5.18 (whose sub-tags already cover reading dx/dt as velocity), adding 5.13 only for a separate kinematics step such as a distance, and a trapezoidal estimate of displacement is 5.8 with 5.13.

subtags.name: Find when acceleration is zero, greatest or least
Use a = v dv/ds to write acceleration in terms of displacement

statements.title: Approximation, bounds, percentage error and estimation
statements.content: Round to decimal places and significant figures, choosing a sensible accuracy for the data and context (for example currency). Find upper and lower bounds of rounded values, calculate percentage errors including the maximum percentage error caused by measurement rounding, and judge whether a calculated result is reasonable.
statements.tagWhen: Rounding to a stated accuracy when the rounding itself earns the mark, the bounds of rounded measurements and the greatest or least value they give a calculated quantity, or a percentage error (including the largest possible one, or working back from a given one). List 1.6 first, adding the statement that produced the estimate (5.8, 5.16, 3.4) second only when its working earns marks in the same part; rounding a 1.4 or 1.7 answer to the nearest dollar is not 1.6, and writing a value as a × 10^k is 1.1.

subtags.name: Round to a given number of decimal places or significant figures
Write down the upper and lower bounds of a rounded value
Find the greatest or least value calculated from rounded measurements
Calculate the percentage error between an approximate and an exact value
Find the largest possible percentage error using the bounds of rounded values
Use a given percentage error to find the possible exact values

statements.title: Amortization and annuities using technology
statements.content: Use technology (the GDC finance solver or a spreadsheet) to solve loan amortization and annuity problems: repayments, number of payments, interest rate, outstanding balance and total interest. In examinations payments are at the end of each period; the annuity formula helps understanding but is not examined.
statements.tagWhen: Any finance-solver problem with regular payments, deposits or withdrawals (PMT ≠ 0): a loan's repayment, term, rate or amount borrowed, the balance outstanding, total paid or total interest, savings built from regular deposits, and annuities paid out until exhausted. A single sum growing or depreciating with PMT = 0 is 1.4 (so a lump sum followed by monthly deposits is 1.4 then 1.7, part by part), and finding a percentage deposit or the amount left to borrow is prior learning.

subtags.name: Find the regular loan repayment, or the deposit needed for a target
Find how many payments repay a loan or exhaust an annuity
Find the interest rate or the amount borrowed or invested
Find the balance owed, or left in an annuity, after some payments
Find the total amount repaid or the total interest paid or earned
Find the value of savings built from regular deposits
Compare loan or savings options and comment on the plan's assumptions

statements.title: Solving linear systems and polynomial equations with technology
statements.content: Use technology to solve systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns and polynomial equations, using the terms zeros and roots. No particular method is required, and exam systems always have a unique solution.
statements.tagWhen: Setting up and solving a system of two or three linear equations, or solving a stated polynomial equation with technology or by hand and keeping the valid roots. Fitting a model's parameters from given points is 2.6 first, with 1.8 second when the system earns its own marks; graph features, non-polynomial equations and a model in context reaching a value are 2.4 (with the model's own statement, 2.5 or 2.9) and f′(x) = 0 is 5.6, and a pair of equations solved inside another statement (u₁ and d, a Voronoi vertex, constants in 5.17, a steady state in 4.19) is not 1.8.

subtags.name: Write a system of linear equations from a context or given conditions
Solve a system of two or three linear equations
Solve a polynomial equation with technology, giving its real roots
Choose the roots that are valid in context or the domain

statements.title: Laws of logarithms
statements.content: Use the laws of logarithms for products, quotients and powers, with base 10 or e in examinations and positive arguments. Apply them to combine or expand expressions and to solve equations.
statements.tagWhen: Using the product, quotient or power law to combine, expand or simplify logarithms, or to solve an equation that needs the laws. Evaluating a logarithm, switching between exponential and log form, or solving a^x = b with technology is 1.5; using a log scale (pH, decibels, magnitude) or linearising data with logs is 2.10, with 1.9 second when applying the laws earns marks (for example finding how many times greater one quantity is than another); an integral or area whose exact answer is simplified with the laws is 5.11 or 5.12 first with 1.9 second.

subtags.name: Combine logarithms into one logarithm or a required form
Expand the logarithm of a product, quotient or power
Solve an equation using the laws of logarithms and exponentiating
Use the quotient law to compare two values on a log scale

statements.title: Simplifying expressions with rational exponents
statements.content: Simplify numerical and algebraic expressions with rational (fractional) exponents, using the laws of exponents and the link between fractional powers and roots, including negative fractional exponents.
statements.tagWhen: Simplifying a numerical or algebraic expression with fractional or negative fractional exponents, or rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers, when the simplification earns its own marks. Rewriting a term as a power before differentiating or integrating belongs to the calculus statement (5.3, 5.5, 5.9 or 5.11); integer exponents are 1.5, and turning a log-log regression line back into y = ax^b is 2.10.

subtags.name: Evaluate or simplify numerical expressions with rational exponents
Simplify algebraic expressions with rational exponents using the exponent laws
Rewrite roots and reciprocals of roots as fractional or negative powers

statements.title: Complex numbers in Cartesian form
statements.content: Introduce i with i² = −1 and complex numbers z = a + bi, with real and imaginary parts, conjugate, modulus and argument. Add, subtract, multiply and divide by hand and with technology, find powers with technology, draw Argand diagrams, and solve real quadratics with negative discriminant, linking to the graph not meeting the x-axis.
statements.tagWhen: Arithmetic with complex numbers in a + bi form (sums, products, quotients, powers of i, conjugates), equating real and imaginary parts, finding |z| or arg z as values, or plotting and reading points on an Argand diagram. Writing z as r cis θ or re^(iθ), working in those forms, describing a multiplication or addition as a rotation, stretch or translation, and adding sinusoids are 1.13; a geometric sequence with a complex ratio is 1.3 (1.11 for its sum to infinity) with 1.12 second.

subtags.name: Add, subtract and multiply complex numbers in Cartesian form
Divide complex numbers by multiplying by the conjugate
Write down and use the complex conjugate, including zz* = |z|²
Equate real and imaginary parts to find unknowns
Find the modulus and argument of a + bi
Plot or read complex numbers on an Argand diagram

statements.title: Polar and exponential forms of complex numbers
statements.content: Write complex numbers in polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ and exponential form re^(iθ), and convert between these and Cartesian form by hand and with technology. Multiply, divide and raise to integer powers in polar or exponential form (finding roots is not required), add sinusoids of equal frequency using complex numbers, and interpret addition as vector addition and multiplication as a rotation with a stretch.
statements.tagWhen: Converting between Cartesian, polar (r cis θ) and exponential (re^(iθ)) forms; multiplying, dividing or raising to integer powers in polar or exponential form; describing multiplication by a complex number as a rotation with a stretch and addition as a translation or vector sum on the Argand diagram; or adding sinusoids of equal frequency as the real or imaginary parts of complex exponentials. Rotations and enlargements written as 2 × 2 matrices are 3.9; plain a + bi arithmetic and |z| or arg z as values are 1.12; roots of complex numbers are not examined.

subtags.name: Convert a + bi to polar or exponential form
Convert polar or exponential form, or a sum, to a + bi
Multiply, divide or find integer powers in polar or exponential form
Read multiplication as rotation with stretch, and addition as translation
Add equal-frequency sinusoids as Re or Im of complex exponentials

statements.title: Matrices: algebra, determinants, inverses and linear systems
statements.content: Use matrix terms (element, row, column, order) and the algebra of matrices: equality, addition, subtraction, scalar and matrix multiplication, with the properties of multiplication and the identity and zero matrices. Find determinants and inverses by hand for 2 × 2 and with technology for larger matrices, and solve Ax = b with the inverse in contexts such as coding messages; A is always invertible in examinations.
statements.tagWhen: Matrix algebra for its own sake: products in the right order, powers, determinants and inverses (2 × 2 by hand, larger with the GDC), unknown entries from a matrix equation, writing a system or recurrence in matrix form, and solving Ax = b with an inverse. A matrix acting as a transformation of the plane is 3.9 first, with 1.14 second only when an inverse, product or matrix equation earns its own marks; adjacency and graph transition matrices are 3.15, Markov chains 4.19, eigenvalues and PDP⁻¹ (including finding P⁻¹) 1.15, and a coupled differential system in matrix form 5.17.

subtags.name: Multiply matrices by hand or with technology, keeping the order correct
Find powers of a matrix with unknown entries and generalise to Aⁿ
Find the determinant of a matrix
Find the inverse of a matrix, including the inverse of a product
Find unknown entries or a vector from a matrix equation
Solve Ax = b using an inverse matrix
Write a linear system or recurrence in matrix form

statements.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalisation of 2 × 2 matrices
statements.content: Find the characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2 × 2 matrices by hand and with technology. Diagonalise 2 × 2 matrices with distinct real eigenvalues and use Mⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹ to find powers in applications such as population movement between two places or predator–prey models.
statements.tagWhen: The characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues or eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrix, verifying an eigenvector, writing M = PDP⁻¹, or using PDⁿP⁻¹ for Mⁿ or Mⁿs₀ in terms of n and its limit as n → ∞. Writing a transition matrix, numerical Tⁿs₀ and a steady state from high powers or from Ts = s are 4.19 (3.15 for a graph), added second when a 1.15 result is read as a long-term state; a coupled system's eigenvalues are 1.15, but its general solution, classification and phase portrait are 5.17.

subtags.name: Find or show the characteristic polynomial from det(M − λI) = 0
Solve the characteristic equation to find the eigenvalues
Find an eigenvector for a given eigenvalue
Verify that a vector is an eigenvector and state its eigenvalue
Write a matrix as PDP⁻¹ with consistent P and D
Use PDⁿP⁻¹ to find Mⁿ or Mⁿs₀ in terms of n
Let n → ∞ in PDⁿP⁻¹ to find the long-term matrix

statements.title: Modelling with linear, quadratic, exponential, power, cubic and sinusoidal functions
statements.content: Using a family of standard functions as models of real situations: linear (including piecewise linear), quadratic (vertex, axis of symmetry, zeros and intercepts, with technology allowed for roots), exponential ka^x + c, ka^(−x) + c and ke^(rx) + c with their horizontal asymptote, direct and inverse variation ax^n (n ∈ ℤ, with the y-axis as an asymptote when n < 0), cubic, and sinusoidal a sin(bx) + d or a cos(bx) + d in degrees. For sinusoids, only amplitude a, period 360°/b and principal axis y = d are needed; converting between sin and cos is not required.
statements.tagWhen: Using a function from the SL model families in context: evaluating it (a plain prediction included), forming a variation or piecewise linear model, or finding and interpreting a family feature such as a quadratic's vertex or axis of symmetry, an exponential's initial value or horizontal asymptote, or a degree sinusoid's amplitude, period and principal axis (so a, b and d). A single straight-line model is 2.1 and a geometric sequence over whole periods is 1.3; parameters found by substituting given points or initial conditions, the choice of model, its domain and its validity are 2.6; when the GDC finds a zero, maximum or intersection (such as when the model reaches a value), add 2.4. At HL, half-life, ln, logistic, radian or phase-shifted sinusoidal and non-linear piecewise models are 2.9, and a function in context that fits none of the families is 2.2 (SL2.2.function-model).

subtags.name: Write or use a piecewise linear model in context
Use a quadratic model, including its axis of symmetry and vertex
Evaluate and interpret an exponential model, including its initial value
Find or interpret the horizontal asymptote of an exponential model
Form and use a direct or inverse variation model y = axⁿ
Use a cubic model in context
Find and use a sinusoidal model's amplitude, period and principal axis

statements.title: The modelling process: choose, fit, test and use a model
statements.content: Following the modelling cycle with the 2.5 (and, at HL, 2.9) function families: choose a suitable model and sensible domain from a context, find its parameters from initial conditions, given points or simultaneous equations solved with technology (up to three linear equations in three unknowns at SL), judge and justify the model, and use it to predict while knowing the risks of extrapolation. Fitting by regression belongs to topic 4, and SL students do not perform non-linear regression.
statements.tagWhen: A step of the modelling cycle earns the marks: choosing or justifying a type of model from the context, data or graph; finding parameters from initial conditions or given points (add 1.8 when solving a linear system for them earns its own marks); stating a reasonable domain; testing a model against data or comparing two models; or explaining a limitation, or how reliable a prediction is, including extrapolation. Evaluating a model or reading its family features is 2.5 (2.9 at HL), even when the question calls it a prediction; fitting the model by regression is 4.4 or 4.13 (SSres and R² comparisons are 4.13), a percentage error between model and data is 1.6, and the reliability of a regression-line prediction is 4.4.

subtags.name: Choose or justify a type of model from context, data or graph
Find a model's parameters from initial conditions or given points
State a reasonable domain for a model in context
Test a model against data, or compare two models
Explain a limitation or an unrealistic feature of a model
Judge how reliable a model's prediction is, including the risk of extrapolation

statements.title: Composite and inverse functions in context
statements.content: Composite functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) set in context, and inverse functions: finding f⁻¹, using f ∘ f⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ f = identity, and restricting a domain (for example to one side of a quadratic's vertex) so an inverse exists.
statements.tagWhen: Forming, evaluating or interpreting a composite function (including substituting one model into another and saying what the order of composition means in context, with values read off a graph or table where needed), solving an equation that involves a composite, or finding an inverse function f⁻¹(x) algebraically with its domain and range. Evaluating f⁻¹(a) by solving f(x) = a, sketching y = f⁻¹(x) as the reflection in y = x, or the domain and range of f itself is 2.2; solving f(x) = f⁻¹(x) or a similar equation with the GDC is 2.4, with 2.7 only when f⁻¹ is found in that part; log laws that earn their own marks while simplifying add 1.9.

subtags.name: Form or interpret a composite function in context, including the order
Evaluate a composite function from formulae, a graph or a table
Solve an equation involving a composite function
Find the inverse function f⁻¹(x) algebraically
State the domain and range of f⁻¹ from those of f

statements.title: Further models: half-life, logarithmic, sinusoidal, logistic and piecewise
statements.content: Extending the SL model families with half-life from exponential models, natural logarithmic models f(x) = a + b ln x, sinusoidal models a sin(b(x − c)) + d in radians (period 2π/b, with c a phase shift), logistic models L/(1 + Ce^(−kx)) with carrying capacity L, and piecewise models, including finding a parameter that makes the pieces join. Students may also meet unfamiliar models defined in a question; the formal definition of continuity is not required.
statements.tagWhen: Using an HL model family: the half-life or doubling time of an exponential model, a natural log model a + b ln x, a sinusoidal model a sin(b(x − c)) + d in radians or with a phase shift, a logistic model (its values, its carrying capacity and why it suits a context), or a piecewise model with non-linear pieces, including a parameter that makes the pieces meet. Other exponential models, degree sinusoids a sin(bx) + d and piecewise linear models stay 2.5 at HL; parameters found from given points are 2.6 (add 2.9 when the value found is the family's own feature, such as L or c); curve fitting by regression is 4.13, adding sinusoids with complex numbers is 1.13, and a model obtained by solving a differential equation is 5.14.

subtags.name: Find a half-life or doubling time from an exponential model
Use a natural logarithmic model f(x) = a + b ln x
Find and use a phase-shifted sinusoidal model in radians
Evaluate or solve a logistic model L/(1 + Ce^(−kx)) in context
Find or interpret the carrying capacity of a logistic model
Write or use a piecewise model with non-linear pieces
Find a parameter that makes the pieces of a piecewise model join

statements.title: Logarithmic scales and linearising data
statements.content: Using logarithms to compress very large or very small numbers onto a manageable scale, and to linearise data: plotting log y against x (semi-log) tests for an exponential relationship and log y against log x (log-log) tests for a power relationship, with the best-fit line giving the parameters. Students interpret semi-log and log-log graphs but are not expected to draw or sketch them.
statements.tagWhen: Using logarithms to rescale or to linearise: comparing two quantities through the difference of their values on a log scale (magnitude, decibels, pH), choosing a semi-log or log-log plot, taking logs of y = abˣ or y = axⁿ to get a straight line, transforming data with logs, or converting a line on log axes back into the model and predicting from it. Evaluating or solving a given log-scale formula is 1.5, and log-law steps that earn their own marks add 1.9; a GDC linear regression on log values is 4.4 (add 2.10 only for the transforming or converting), while fitting an exponential or power curve directly by regression, with R² or SSres, is 4.13.

subtags.name: Compare quantities from the difference of their log-scale values
Choose the semi-log or log-log plot that makes the data linear
Take logs of an exponential or power model to linearise it
Transform data with logarithms ready for a linear fit
Convert a line for log data into an exponential or power model
Predict an original value from a linearised model by undoing the logs

statements.title: Arc length and sector area in degrees
statements.content: Arc length and sector area of a circle with the angle in degrees, as the fraction θ/360 of the circumference 2πr or the area πr². Radians are not used at SL.
statements.tagWhen: Arc length, sector perimeter or sector area with the angle in degrees, including working back to r or θ, segments and other regions built from sectors, the angle turned by a clock hand or wheel, and a sector folded into a cone. With θ in radians, or a radian answer required, it is 3.7; add 3.2 when ½ab sin C or the cosine rule earns marks (as in a segment) and 3.1 for the cone's volume or surface area, while a degree sinusoid such as h = a cos(bt) + d is 2.5.

subtags.name: Find arc length or sector perimeter, or solve for r or θ
Find sector area, or solve for r or θ
Find areas or perimeters of segments and regions built from sectors
Fold a sector into a cone: arc length equals base circumference
Find the angle turned from a fraction of a turn or rate

statements.title: Equations of perpendicular bisectors
statements.content: Finding the equation of the perpendicular bisector of a segment, given either its two endpoints or the equation of the line containing it together with its midpoint. Uses midpoints, perpendicular gradients and the forms of a straight line from 2.1.
statements.tagWhen: Finding the gradient or equation of a perpendicular bisector from two endpoints (or from the segment's line and midpoint), including a Voronoi edge between two given sites and 'show that' versions; the perpendicular gradient is part of 3.5, not 2.1. A midpoint on its own is 2.1, as is a point where a bisector meets a road or another bisector outside a Voronoi diagram; in a Voronoi diagram, vertices, nearest sites, cells and added sites are 3.6, added to 3.5 only when that reasoning earns marks in the same part.

subtags.name: Find a perpendicular bisector's equation from two endpoints, or line and midpoint
Find a perpendicular bisector's gradient as the negative reciprocal
Write down a horizontal or vertical perpendicular bisector by inspection

statements.title: Voronoi diagrams
statements.content: Voronoi diagrams: sites, edges, vertices and cells, and adding a new site. Uses include finding a boundary equation from given site coordinates, the nearest site to a point, cell areas, nearest neighbour interpolation and the 'toxic waste dump' problem, whose answer is at a vertex where three edges meet. Students do not construct bisectors geometrically.
statements.tagWhen: Reasoning with a Voronoi diagram: what cells, edges and vertices mean, the nearest site to a point (from the diagram or by comparing distances), locating a site from an edge, a vertex equidistant from three sites, drawing or updating the cells when a site is added, cell areas, nearest neighbour interpolation, the toxic waste dump problem and criticising the model. The equation of an edge between two sites is 3.5 (add 3.6 only if Voronoi reasoning in that part earns marks), and a cell's area or angle by the sine or cosine rule adds 3.2.

subtags.name: Identify the nearest site to a point, from the diagram or distances
Interpret cells, edges and vertices in context and criticise the model

statements.title: Radian measure
statements.content: Definition of the radian and conversion between degrees and radians, with answers as exact multiples of π or decimals. Arc length l = rθ and sector area A = ½r²θ with θ in radians.
statements.tagWhen: Converting between degrees and radians, or arc length l = rθ, sector area ½r²θ and regions built from them with θ in radians, including equations in r and θ from given conditions and an angle turned at a given rate. The same work in degrees is 3.4, and radians used only as the unit of a sinusoidal model (2.9), calculus with trig functions (5.9, 5.11), a rotation matrix (3.9), circular motion (3.12) or a volume of revolution through 2π (5.12) are not 3.7.

statements.title: The unit circle, the Pythagorean identity, the ambiguous case and graphical trigonometric equations
statements.content: cos θ and sin θ defined as coordinates on the unit circle, the graphs of sin x and cos x built from it, tan θ = sin θ / cos θ and the identity cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. The ambiguous case of the sine rule, and solving trigonometric equations graphically on a finite interval. Exact values are not assessed.
statements.tagWhen: Rewriting an expression with cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 or tan θ = sin θ/cos θ (often inside a derivative or a matrix product), the ambiguous case of the sine rule (two possible triangles, by the sine rule or a cosine-rule quadratic), or solving a trig equation for an angle on a finite interval, graphically or with inverse trig. One angle in a triangle is 3.2 and sinusoidal model parameters are 2.5 or 2.9; a model value found by intersecting graphs on the GDC is 2.4 with the model statement, as at SL (where a two-triangle cosine-rule case is 3.2).

subtags.name: Rewrite or simplify an expression using cos²θ + sin²θ = 1

Solve a trig equation on a finite interval, finding every solution

statements.title: Matrix transformations of the plane
statements.content: 2 × 2 matrices for reflections, horizontal and vertical stretches, enlargements and rotations about the origin, with translations added as a vector, in the form Ax + b. Compositions of these, iterated transformations such as simple fractals, and the determinant as the area scale factor: image area = |det A| × object area.
statements.tagWhen: Using a 2 × 2 matrix as a transformation of the plane: writing or describing the matrix of a reflection, stretch, enlargement or rotation about the origin, finding images or original points under Ax + b, composing, decomposing or iterating transformations (including fixed points and simple fractals), or using |det A| as the area scale factor. Matrix arithmetic with no geometric meaning is 1.14 (add it here only when an inverse or a matrix equation earns its own marks); rotations and enlargements done by multiplying complex numbers are 1.13, and transformations of the graph of a function are 2.8.

statements.title: Vectors and scalars: representation and components
statements.content: Vectors and scalars, vectors as directed line segments and in component (column or i, j, k) form, the zero vector and −v. Sums, differences, scalar multiples and resultants, both algebraically and geometrically; parallel vectors; magnitude; position vectors; and rescaling to a unit vector or to a given magnitude.
statements.tagWhen: Vectors built from components without any product: column or i, j, k form, a displacement AB = b − a or a position vector, sums, differences, scalar multiples and resultants, magnitudes and distances found as magnitudes, unit vectors or vectors of a given length, and parallel or equal vectors (for example to show a quadrilateral is a parallelogram). Distances and midpoints from coordinates alone are 3.1, scalar and vector products and the angles and areas they give are 3.13, and speed or position in a motion context is 3.12.

statements.title: Vector equation of a line
statements.content: The vector equation of a line r = a + λb in two and three dimensions, where a is a point on the line and b a direction vector, and conversion to parametric form x = x₀ + λl, y = y₀ + λm, z = z₀ + λn.
statements.tagWhen: Lines in two or three dimensions where the parameter is not time: writing r = a + λb from a point and a direction or from two points, converting to parametric form, checking whether a point lies on a line, finding where two lines meet, or finding the point on a line closest to a given point (add 3.13 when the scalar product earns marks). When the parameter is time and objects move, tag 3.12 instead; the angle between two lines is 3.13, and the image of a line under a matrix is 3.9 (add 3.11 when writing the new equation earns marks).

statements.title: Vector kinematics
statements.content: Vectors in kinematics: constant-velocity motion r = r₀ + vt in two and three dimensions, positions and times, intersections and collisions, relative position AB and closest approach. Also variable velocity in two dimensions, with projectile and circular motion as special cases, and time shifts written with t − a.
statements.tagWhen: Motion described by vectors with t as time: using r = r₀ + vt, speed as |v| and the direction of motion, whether objects meet or collide, the relative position r_B − r_A and the time and distance of closest approach (the minimum, by GDC or calculus, belongs here and not to 2.4), a later start written with t − a, and variable velocity in two dimensions by differentiating or integrating vectors, including projectile and circular motion. statements.title: Scalar and vector products
statements.content: The scalar product v · w = |v||w| cos θ, the angle between two vectors, the acute angle between two lines and the perpendicularity test v · w = 0. The vector product v × w with direction by the right-hand rule, |v × w| as the area of a parallelogram or triangle, and the components of a parallel and perpendicular to b. Proofs and general properties are not required.
statements.tagWhen: Products of vectors: computing v · w, the angle between two vectors or the acute angle between two lines, using v · w = 0 to show or impose perpendicularity, computing v × w or a vector perpendicular to two vectors, using |v × w| for the area of a triangle or parallelogram or a turning effect, or the component of one vector along another. Forming the vectors is 3.10 and an angle found by the cosine rule is 3.2; when a scalar product locates the closest point on a line, tag 3.11 (or 3.12 for moving objects) first and add 3.13.

statements.title: Graph theory: vertices, edges, degree and types of graph
statements.content: Basic graph theory: vertices, edges, adjacency, degree; simple, complete, weighted and directed graphs with in-degree and out-degree; connected and strongly connected graphs; subgraphs and trees. Representing real structures such as maps, networks and circuits as graphs.
statements.tagWhen: Describing a graph: drawing a graph, weighted graph or directed graph to represent a real network, finding vertex degrees (in- and out-degrees for a directed graph), or deciding with a reason whether a graph is simple, complete, connected, strongly connected or a tree. Adjacency matrices and walk counts are 3.15, and Eulerian and Hamiltonian questions and all the algorithms are 3.16, even when the reason given is a degree argument.

statements.title: Adjacency matrices, walks and transition matrices for graphs
statements.content: Adjacency matrices for graphs and directed graphs, walks and counting walks of length k (or up to k) using powers of the adjacency matrix, weighted adjacency tables, and transition matrices for strongly connected undirected or directed graphs, with Google PageRank as an application.
statements.tagWhen: Matrices built from a graph: writing, completing or reading an adjacency matrix (loops and multiple edges included) or drawing its graph, counting walks of length k with Mᵏ or up to length k with a sum of powers, deciding which vertices can be reached in k steps, or building the transition matrix of a random walk on a graph from the edges at each vertex. Transition matrices with probabilities given in context, Tⁿs₀ and steady states are 4.19 (so a long-run proportion or n-step probability for a random walk on a graph, as in PageRank, is 4.19, with 3.15 added when building the matrix from the graph earns marks in the same part), eigenvalues and eigenvectors found by hand are 1.15, and a table of least distances is 3.16.

statements.title: Graph algorithms: Eulerian and Hamiltonian routes, spanning trees, Chinese postman and travelling salesman
statements.content: Walks, trails, paths, circuits and cycles; deciding whether Eulerian trails or circuits exist; Hamiltonian paths and cycles. Minimum spanning trees by Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms (including Prim's on a matrix). The Chinese postman problem with up to four odd vertices, with explanation of why it works; and the travelling salesman problem with a table of least distances, nearest-neighbour upper bounds and deleted-vertex lower bounds.
statements.tagWhen: Routes and algorithms on graphs: deciding from vertex degrees whether an Eulerian trail or circuit exists and finding one, Hamiltonian paths and cycles, minimum spanning trees by Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm (Prim's also on a table), the Chinese postman problem (pairing odd vertices, repeated edges, the minimum length and a valid route) and the travelling salesman problem (a table of least distances, nearest-neighbour upper bounds, deleted-vertex lower bounds and the best interval for the optimum). Use the Kruskal or Prim sub-tag only when the part names the algorithm or marks the edge order; a degree asked as a fact is 3.14, adjacency matrices are 3.15, and bounds from rounded edge lengths are 1.6.

statements.title: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
statements.content: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rs, found with technology, with tied data values given the average of their ranks; knowing that Pearson's r measures only linear association while rs measures any monotonic association, and that rs is less affected by outliers. Deriving either coefficient is not required.
statements.tagWhen: Ranking data (tied values take the mean of their ranks), finding or interpreting Spearman's rs, choosing between rs and r (monotonic versus linear association, outliers, a changed value that keeps its rank), or testing rs against a given critical value. Pearson's r, the scatter diagram and the y-on-x line are 4.4, and a test of ρ = 0 with Pearson's r is 4.18; a part that finds both r and rs takes 4.4 and 4.10.

statements.title: Hypothesis testing: χ² tests and the t-test
statements.content: Writing null and alternative hypotheses and reaching conclusions with significance levels and p-values; χ² tests for independence (contingency tables up to 4 × 4, degrees of freedom, critical values) and goodness of fit, using expected and observed frequencies; the pooled two-sample t-test for unpaired samples from normal populations, one- or two-tailed. Exam tests are upper-tail at 1%, 5% or 10%, the statistic and p-value come from technology, and expected frequencies exceed 5.
statements.tagWhen: A χ² test for independence or goodness of fit, or a pooled two-sample t-test: its hypotheses, expected frequencies, degrees of freedom, statistic or p-value, conclusion, conditions (normal populations with equal variances, expected frequencies above 5) or the meaning of a p-value, adding 4.8, 4.9 or 4.17 when expected frequencies need that model's probabilities. One-sample, paired, binomial, Poisson and ρ = 0 tests, critical regions and Type I or II errors are 4.18, and at HL combining cells so expected frequencies exceed 5, or losing a degree of freedom for each estimated parameter, is 4.12.

statements.title: Designing data collection; reliability and validity
statements.content: Designing valid data collection, including surveys and questionnaires with structured, unbiased and precise questions; choosing relevant variables and data to analyse; grouping numerical data into categories for a χ² test so that expected frequencies exceed 5, and reducing the degrees of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data; the difference between reliability and validity, with test-retest and parallel-forms reliability, and content and criterion-related validity.
statements.tagWhen: Designing or criticising data collection (survey questions, choice of variables), reliability (test-retest, parallel forms) or validity (content, criterion-related), or adapting a χ² test: grouping data or combining categories so every expected frequency exceeds 5, and subtracting a degree of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data. Sampling methods, bias in a sample and outliers are 4.1; the χ² test itself is 4.11, listed first when combining cells is only a step in performing it, and a correlation coefficient used to judge validity or reliability is 4.10 or 4.4 with 4.12 for the judgement.

statements.title: Non-linear regression and the coefficient of determination
statements.content: Fitting least squares regression curves with technology: linear, quadratic, cubic, exponential, power and sine models; the sum of square residuals SSres as a measure of fit; the coefficient of determination R² as the proportion of variation in y explained by the model, with R² = r² for linear models. R² alone is not a reliable way to choose between models; the formula R² = 1 − SSres/SStot is not examined.
statements.tagWhen: Fitting a least squares quadratic, cubic, exponential, power or sine regression model with technology, finding or minimising the sum of square residuals, or finding, interpreting or comparing R² (including R² = r² for a linear model). The y-on-x line and Pearson's r are 4.4; a linear regression on log-transformed data (ln y on x, ln y on ln x) is 2.10 with 4.4; using the fitted curve to predict or criticising it in context is 2.6 (with 2.9 for the HL families).

statements.title: Linear combinations of random variables and unbiased estimates
statements.content: Expectation and variance of a linear transformation aX + b; the expected value of any linear combination of random variables and the variance of a linear combination of independent random variables; x̄ as an unbiased estimate of μ and s²ₙ₋₁ = n/(n − 1) × s²ₙ as an unbiased estimate of σ². Proofs that these estimators are unbiased are not examined.

A probability for a combination of normal variables or a sample mean is 4.15, which includes its mean and variance; adding to or multiplying every value of a data set is 4.3; the mean and variance of a single binomial variable are 4.8.

statements.title: Combining normal variables and the central limit theorem
statements.content: Any linear combination of independent normal variables is normal, so X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) when X ~ N(μ, σ²); the central limit theorem says the sample mean is approximately normal for large samples from any distribution, with n > 30 taken as large enough in exams.
statements.tagWhen: A probability, value or distribution for a linear combination of independent normal variables (a total, a difference, several independent copies), for a sample mean using X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n), or for the mean of a large sample (n > 30) by the central limit theorem; finding the combination's mean and variance is part of 4.15. E and Var asked for on their own are 4.14, a single normal variable is 4.9, and a critical region or error probability for a test of a mean is 4.18, which includes using X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n).

statements.title: Confidence intervals for a mean
statements.content: Confidence intervals for the mean of a normal population, using the normal distribution when σ is known and the t-distribution when σ is unknown, whatever the sample size, and interpreting the interval in context.
statements.tagWhen: Finding a confidence interval for a population mean with technology (z when σ is known, t when σ is unknown), stating the conditions for it to be valid, or interpreting it in context, such as whether a claimed mean is plausible. The unbiased estimates that feed it are 4.14, and a hypothesis test of the mean is 4.18; tag by the method the question asks for.

statements.title: The Poisson distribution
statements.content: The Poisson distribution as a model for independent events occurring at a uniform average rate, with mean and variance both equal to λ; the sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson; choosing between normal, binomial and Poisson models in context. Proofs of mean and variance are not required.
statements.tagWhen: Poisson probabilities (exact or cumulative, with technology), rescaling the mean to another interval, adding the means of independent Poisson variables, finding λ or a least number from a given probability, or justifying, rejecting or choosing a Poisson model (independent events at a constant rate, mean equal to variance). A count of successes in n independent trials is 4.8 even when p is a Poisson probability, with 4.17 added when that probability is found in the same part; tests and critical regions for a Poisson mean are 4.18, and E and Var of a combination such as 3X + 5Y are 4.14.

statements.title: Critical regions, tests for a mean, a proportion or a correlation, and type I and II errors
statements.content: Critical values and critical regions; tests for a population mean using z when σ is known and t when σ is unknown, with matched pairs treated as one sample of differences; one-tailed tests for a proportion (binomial) and a mean (Poisson); testing ρ = 0 with technology; Type I and Type II errors and their probabilities for normal (known variance), binomial and Poisson tests. statements.title: Transition matrices and Markov chains
statements.content: Markov chains: transition diagrams and transition matrices T with Tᵢⱼ the probability of moving from state j to state i, initial state matrices, and the state after n steps sₙ = Tⁿs₀; regular Markov chains; steady-state and long-term probabilities found by high powers of T or by solving linear equations, seen as the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1.

statements.title: Stationary points: local maxima and minima
statements.content: Finding where a curve has zero gradient by solving f′(x) = 0, with technology used to produce f′ and to solve, and identifying local maximum and minimum points. A maximum or minimum read off the GDC graph of f with no derivative is 2.4, and optimising a quantity in context over a variable someone chooses is 5.7 instead (if the question says local maximum, local minimum or stationary point, use 5.6); add 5.3 or 5.9 only when the derivative is found in the same part, and at HL f″ checks are 5.10 and dy/dx = 0 for an unknown solution curve of a differential equation is 5.15.

statements.title: Optimisation in context
statements.content: Solving optimisation problems in context with calculus and technology: maximising profit or volume, minimising cost or material, including setting up the function from a constraint such as a fixed volume or surface area. Kinematics optimisation is not set at SL.
statements.tagWhen: An optimisation problem in context: making a quantity someone wants as large or small as possible (profit, cost, volume, area, material) by choosing a dimension, price, quantity or angle, including writing it as a function of one variable from a constraint such as a fixed volume, finding the optimal value of the variable and the optimum, by calculus or on the GDC (do not add 5.6 or 2.4 for these steps), using a given optimum to find a parameter, or showing that a value is or is not optimal. statements.title: Approximating areas with the trapezoidal rule
statements.content: Estimating an area with the trapezoidal rule using intervals of equal width, from a function or from a table of data such as measurements of an irregular shape. Includes comparing the estimate with the true value and saying whether it is an over- or underestimate.
statements.tagWhen: Estimating with the trapezoidal rule and equal intervals, from a table or graph of values or from a function evaluated at the interval ends: an area, or an accumulated quantity such as a total from a rate, a displacement from velocities or a volume from cross-sections; choosing h and the right ordinates; and explaining whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate or how to make it more accurate. The exact value by integration is 5.5 (or 5.11 or 5.12 at HL) and the percentage error between estimate and exact value is 1.6, not 5.8; add 5.12 when the rule is applied to πr² or πx² for a volume and 5.13 when it estimates a displacement from velocity.

statements.title: Further differentiation: standard derivatives, chain, product and quotient rules, related rates
statements.content: Differentiating sin x, cos x, tan x, eˣ, ln x and xⁿ for rational n, and combining them with the chain, product and quotient rules. Applying derivatives to related rates of change and, through the link to 5.6 and 5.7, to stationary points and optimisation.

Integer powers alone are 5.3, never both for the same derivative; what the derivative is then used for adds its own statement (5.4 tangent or normal, 5.6 turning point, 5.7 optimisation, 5.10 second derivative, 5.13 straight-line motion, 3.12 vector motion), and a differential equation formed from a related rate is 5.14 with 5.9.

statements.title: The second derivative and the second derivative test
statements.content: The second derivative in both notations, d²y/dx² and f″(x), and its use in the second derivative test for maxima and minima. Concave-up (f″ > 0) and concave-down (f″ < 0), and points of inflexion as points where the concavity changes, interpreted in context.
statements.tagWhen: Finding or using the second derivative d²y/dx² or f″(x): concavity from its sign, including to confirm that a stationary point or an optimum is a maximum or minimum; points of inflexion where f″ = 0 and changes sign, found algebraically or as a turning point of f′ on the GDC (not 2.4); and where a rate of change is greatest or least (steepest, fastest rising), interpreted in context. Add 5.9 when getting f″ needs the chain, product or quotient rule; classifying a turning point from f′ or a graph is 5.6, a sketch that merely shows the right curvature is not 5.10, zero or greatest acceleration of a particle is 5.13, and second-order differential equations are 5.17 or 5.18.

statements.title: Further integration: standard integrals, inspection and substitution
statements.content: Definite and indefinite integrals of xⁿ for rational n (including n = −1, giving ln x), sin x, cos x, 1/cos²x and eˣ. Integrating by inspection or by the substitution u = g(x) for integrals of the form ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx, including linear insides such as sin(2x + 5).
statements.tagWhen: Integrating by hand anything beyond integer powers of x: xⁿ for rational n including 1/x (giving ln x), sin x, cos x, 1/cos²x and eˣ, composites with a linear inside such as cos(2x) or 1/(x + 2), and ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx by inspection or u = g(x), whether indefinite, with a constant from a given point, or as an exact definite integral. Integer powers only, and definite integrals done on the GDC, are 5.5 (never both for one integral); add 5.5 only when setting up an area integral earns its own marks, 5.12 for an area below the axis, against the y-axis or a volume, 5.13 when the integral gives displacement or velocity, and integrals inside separation of variables are 5.14 (add 5.11 only when an inspection or substitution integral there earns its own marks).

statements.title: Areas against either axis and volumes of revolution
statements.content: Areas of regions bounded by a curve and either the x-axis or the y-axis over a given interval, including parts below the axis where the integral is negative. Volumes of revolution about the x-axis (V = ∫ πy² dx) or the y-axis (V = ∫ πx² dy).
statements.tagWhen: Areas against an axis that 5.5 does not cover, namely a region partly or wholly below the x-axis (split at the roots or use |f(x)|) or a region against the y-axis found by integrating x with respect to y, and volumes of revolution through 2π about the x-axis (π∫y² dx) or the y-axis (π∫x² dy): writing the integral, rearranging the curve for x, building a region from several curves or cylinders, using a variable limit (such as a depth of liquid) and evaluating, usually on the GDC. An area wholly above the x-axis, or between two curves above it, is 5.5; add 5.11 when the integral is done by hand with HL integrals, 5.8 when the volume is estimated by the trapezoidal rule, 5.9 for a related rate such as dh/dt from the volume, and 2.7 when a separate part asks for an inverse function.

statements.title: Setting up differential equations and separating variables
statements.content: Forming a differential equation from a description in context, such as a rate proportional to the amount present, and solving it by separating the variables. Includes the general solution (with an arbitrary constant), particular solutions from given conditions, and the exponential model as the solution of dy/dx = ky.
statements.tagWhen: Forming a differential equation from a context, interpreting the terms, parameters or limiting value of a differential equation model (single or coupled), or solving one by separating variables and finding its constants from given conditions. dy/dx = f(x) solved by direct integration is 5.5 or 5.11; add 5.11 only when an inspection or substitution integral inside the separation earns its own marks and 5.9 when the equation comes from a related rate (dh/dt from dV/dt); predicting from the finished solution, or using a given exponential or logistic function, is 2.5/2.6 or 2.9, and equilibrium points of a coupled system are 5.17.

statements.title: Slope fields
statements.content: Using and interpreting slope fields for dy/dx = f(x, y): drawing short segments with the gradient at grid points, matching fields to equations, sketching solution curves through a given point and reading features such as equilibrium solutions and long-term behaviour.
statements.tagWhen: Working with a slope field for dy/dx = f(x, y): evaluating dy/dx at a point, matching a field to its equation, sketching the solution curve through a point, or setting dy/dx = 0 to find the curve where solutions turn (5.15, not 5.6, as no function is known). Solving the equation is 5.14 and an Euler estimate 5.16, even within a slope-field question; add 5.4 when writing a tangent's equation earns marks, and gradients of phase-plane trajectories are 5.17.

statements.title: Euler's method for single and coupled first-order equations
statements.content: Euler's method for approximate solutions of dy/dx = f(x, y) and of coupled systems dx/dt = f₁(x, y, t), dy/dt = f₂(x, y, t), such as predator-prey models. Values are generated with a spreadsheet or GDC; students should understand the step-by-step method, the effect of the step size and how to interpret the output.
statements.tagWhen: Euler's method for dy/dx = f(x, y) or for two first-order coupled equations given as such (linear or not): writing and iterating the update formulae, reading maxima, minima, crossing times or trends from the output or a trajectory plotted from it, and judging accuracy, step size or why the method fails. Euler's method on a second-order equation is 5.18; exact solutions are 5.14 or 5.17 and equilibrium points 5.17, and a percentage error against an exact or measured value adds 1.6.

statements.title: Phase portraits for coupled linear differential equations
statements.content: Phase portraits for dx/dt = ax + by, dy/dt = cx + dy with distinct non-zero eigenvalues: classifying the origin from the eigenvalues (real, complex or purely imaginary), sketching trajectories and identifying equilibrium points, stability and saddle points. Exact solutions are only needed for real distinct eigenvalues.
statements.tagWhen: Phase-plane work on coupled systems: the general or particular solution of a linear system from its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, classifying the equilibrium (node, saddle, spiral or centre; stable or unstable), equilibrium points (non-linear models too), dy/dx or the direction of motion at a point, and sketching, matching or reading phase portraits and long-term behaviour. Finding the eigenvalues or eigenvectors themselves is 1.15 (tag 1.15 alone when that is all a part asks, and add it to 5.17 when that working earns marks in a part that also uses them); Euler iterations and trajectories plotted from them are 5.16, and for a second-order equation add 5.18 when the conversion or the meaning of dx/dt earns marks.

statements.title: Second-order differential equations by Euler's method
statements.content: Approximate solutions of second-order equations d²x/dt² = f(x, dx/dt, t) by rewriting them as the coupled system dx/dt = y, dy/dt = f(x, y, t) and applying Euler's method. Equations of the form d²x/dt² + a dx/dt + bx = 0 can also be studied with the phase portraits of 5.17; the equation is always given in examinations.
statements.tagWhen: Second-order equations d²x/dt² = f(x, dx/dt, t): rewriting as dx/dt = y, dy/dt = f(x, y, t) (or in matrix form, or showing the reverse), applying Euler's method to that system, and reading x and y = dx/dt as displacement and velocity, including initial and long-term values and how x varies with t. The eigenvalue solution and phase portrait of d²x/dt² + a dx/dt + bx = 0 are 5.17 (with 1.15 for bare eigenvalues), adding 5.18 for the conversion or the dx/dt condition; Euler's method on a first-order system that needed no conversion is 5.16, and other kinematics such as a = v dv/ds is 5.13.
